'''''Megathyrsus maximus''''', known as '''Guinea grass''' and '''green panic grass''',<ref name=GRIN/> is a large [[perennial]] [[bunch grass]] that is native to [[Africa]] and [[Yemen]]. It has been [[Introduced species|introduced]] in the [[tropics]] [[Pantropical|around the world]]. It has previously been called ''Urochloa maxima'' and ''Panicum maximum''. It was moved to the genus ''[[Megathyrsus]]'' in 2003.<ref name=Simon2003/><ref name=gm>[http://herbarium.usu.edu/treatments/Megathyrsus.htm ''Megathyrsus''.] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160304083522/http://herbarium.usu.edu/treatments/Megathyrsus.htm |date=2016-03-04 }} Grass Manual. Flora of North America.</ref>

==Description==
''Megathyrsus maximus'' grows naturally in open [[grassland]]s, usually under or near [[tree]]s and [[shrub]]s and [[Riparian zone|along riverbanks]]. It can withstand [[wildfire]] and [[drought]]. The species has broad morphological and agronomic variability, ranging in height from {{convert|0.5|to|3.5|m|ft|abbr=on}}, with {{convert|5|-|10|cm|in|abbr=on}} stems. The [[polyploid]] plant also can reproduce through [[apomixis]], effectively cloning itself through seed.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Rhodes |first1=Aaron C. |last2=Plowes |first2=Robert M. |last3=Martins |first3=Dino J. |last4=Ng’Iru |first4=Ivy |last5=Gilbert |first5=Lawrence E. |date=2022-11-11 |title=The invasiveness of Guinea grass (Megathyrsus maximus) is characterized by habitat and differing herbivore assemblages in its native and invaded range |url=https://zenodo.org/records/7316384/files/NB_article_87069.pdf |journal=NeoBiota |language=en |volume=78 |pages=25–44 |doi=10.3897/neobiota.78.87069 |doi-access=free |issn=1314-2488}}</ref> [[Panicle]]s are open, with as many as 9,000 [[seed]]s per plant.

==Uses==
It can be used as a long-term foraging grass if [[Grazing|grazed]] consistently and if fertilized. It is well suited for cut-and-carry, a practice in which grass is harvested and brought to a [[ruminant]] animal in an enclosed system. Shade tolerance makes it suited to coexisting with trees in [[agroforestry]]. Some varieties have been used successfully for making [[silage]] and hay. The leaves contain good levels of [[protein]] (6–25% depending on age and nitrogen supply).

==Invasive species==
In some places, such as South [[Texas]] and [[Hawai'i]],<ref name=Guardian10082023>{{cite news |last=Anguiano |first=Dani |url=https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2023/aug/09/hawaii-wildfires-maui-explainer |title=Hawaii wildfires: how did the deadly Maui fire start and what caused it? Rapidly moving fires that exploded on Tuesday night on the island of Maui have killed dozens and displaced thousands |work=[[The Guardian]] |date=August 10, 2023 |access-date=August 10, 2023 |archive-date=August 10, 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230810010137/https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2023/aug/09/hawaii-wildfires-maui-explainer}}</ref> it is an [[Invasive species|invasive]] [[weed]] that suppresses or displaces local [[native plants]] and is a fire hazard.<ref>{{Cite news |first=Benjamin |last=Shingler |date=August 9, 2023 |title=Why Maui's deadly wildfires spread so quickly |publisher=CBC News |url=https://www.cbc.ca/news/climate/maui-fires-explainer-1.6932886 |url-status=live |access-date=August 10, 2023 |archive-date=August 10, 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230810202252/http://www.cbc.ca/news/climate/maui-fires-explainer-1.6932886 }}</ref>

In the Australian state of [[Queensland]], the [[Queensland Acclimatisation Society]] introduced Guinea grass to 22 locations between 1865 and 1869.<ref>Clements, R. J. and E. F. Henzell. (2010).[http://www.tropicalgrasslands.asn.au/Tropical%20Grasslands%20Journal%20archive/PDFs/Vol_44%20%281_2_3_4%29/Vol%2044%20%284%29%20Henzell%20%20Clements%20221.pdf Pasture research and development in northern Australia: an ongoing scientific adventure.] ''Tropical Grasslands'' 44, 221–30.</ref>
